#492. Rome MIA Market Takeaways, From Bracing for Netflix Fallout to Italy’s Production Slump and European Producers Fighting Back

The 12th edition of Rome’s MIA Market came to a close on Friday with market head Gaia Tridente heralding “a stronger, renewed edition of MIA, with a more ambitious and expanded program,” that saw a high-powered cohort of European and global industry guests — including Banijay Entertainment CEO Marco Bassetti, Studiocanal CEO Anna Marsh, Bad Wolf CEO Jane Tranter, and filmmakers Edward Berger (“All Quiet on the Western Front”) and Asif Kapadia (“Amy”) — arriving for a lively week in the Eternal City. Related Stories Emmys Move to Prime Video in Six-Year, Global Deal Worth Around $15 Million a Year

This year’s market expanded its footprint beyond its traditional home in the Palazzo Barberini and adjacent Cinema Barberini, incorporating several new venues along the elegant Via Veneto — of “La Dolce Vita” fame — and in the process “making the city itself an integral part of the market’s identity and experience,” according to Tridente. Popular on Variety

She went on to say that those changes represented “probably been one of the biggest transformations of MIA, and certainly one of the most challenging from an organizational perspective.”

“We have completely reimagined the geography of the market, creating a new industry district in the heart of Rome, with Palazzo Barberini as our main hub and a network of venues along Via Veneto,” she said. “The idea was not simply to accommodate a growing market. We wanted to create a different experience for our participants, with dedicated spaces for the different activities, while keeping everything within walking distance.

“In many ways, the entire neighborhood becomes part of the market. I believe this new structure gives MIA a much stronger identity and offers us room to grow,” she continued. “And I have to say, being able to experience Rome in this way is something quite special. The city is not just a backdrop for MIA; it is part of what makes the market unique.”

This year’s event witnessed several other significant changes, including the introduction of a new gap-financing market for animation series and the launch of a dedicated strand showcasing the range of financial tools available to European producers and the growing role of equity capital in film and television production (more on that below).

The market also shifted its dates to take place alongside the Rome Film Festival, as well as Alice nella Città, an autonomous festival that runs parallel to the Rome fest.

“The decision was primarily part of a broader strategy to strengthen Rome’s position as an international hub for the audiovisual industry,” said Tridente, by “bringing these three events closer together in the calendar and creating greater opportunities for collaboration and synergies between the industry and the festivals.

“MIA remains an independent international industry market, with its own identity and objectives, but I believe that having the market and the two festivals taking place at the same time can generate additional value for the entire industry, from producers and distributors to filmmakers and international buyers,” she added.

Here are Variety’s takeaways from a busy week in Rome:

Unprecedented turbulence, untapped potential

The 12th edition of MIA marked the first industry confab to take place since the Red Wedding-style bloodbath at Netflix, which saw the Los Gatos-based streamer ax 1,000 employees — around 6% of its workforce — including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and head of film Dan Lin, whose firing was announced on Monday just hours before MIA attendees gathered for an opening reception in Rome’s lavish Palazzo Barberini.

The firings were the latest in a series of shake-ups, retrenchments and mergers — including Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to form Skydance Corp. — that are recasting the shape of the industry, with many still puzzling over what such seismic shifts will mean for the landscape of production and distribution moving forward.

For some execs in Rome, such turbulence invites a chance to think outside the box — and seize the moment. “In my world, mergers represent opportunity. Contraction represents opportunity,” said Roeg Sutherland, who is co-head of CAA’s media finance department and its international film group. “Financiers see that as a moment where people will be opportunistic.” Anna Marsh, the CEO of Studiocanal and the deputy CEO and chief content officer for Canal+, which in the past year alone has swooped up several companies across two continents, insisted such M&As are essential for survival amid the disruptions of corporate consolidations, shifting consumption habits, emerging technologies and other industry turbulence.

“The audience is so tough that we constantly need to be looking at ourselves in the mirror,” she said. “It’s really important to have a fresh perspective. People that are going to challenge the status quo. Because the business is moving so fast.”

For European producers, there’s also an upside when pan-European studios like Banijay, Mediawan and Vuelta go on a buying spree. “In an ideal world, a group gives you business affairs, cash flow, finance,” said Lorenzo De Maio, president of De Maio Entertainment. “Because the market is so challenging, being part of a group does give you a little bit more support. And usually, the creative stays with the producer.”

In a keynote speech in Rome, Marco Bassetti, CEO of London-based Banijay Entertainment, the world’s largest independent studio, said that “the major debate currently taking place in Europe … is about recognizing and providing compensation for creativity.” That debate is taking different forms, from the ramped-up efforts of European producers to retain IP rights to the ongoing calls for quotas that would require global streamers to invest a portion of their revenues into local productions. “The reality is that we have no ownership, and it’s extremely difficult to secure any, though things are starting to open up a bit,” Bassetti said. “Ultimately, [the studios and the streamers] still have total control.”

Across the board, producers are feeling the squeeze. “We all know that the business has gotten quite challenging right now,” said De Maio. “Distribution advances have gone down. Gaps are harder to finance …. Buyers, both in film and TV, have become very specific with their mandates. Production costs are going up.” Meanwhile, the dizzying pace of shake-ups in C-suites and boardrooms has made it harder than ever to shepherd a project from script to screen; the commissioner who greenlights a project one day might be pink-slipped the next. “Sometimes the decision is made for you,” said Andrea Calderwood, of the U.K.’s “Die My Love” producer Potboiler Productions, on learning to adapt to uncertainty. “Sometimes you might think you’re choosing, but often the circumstances choose you.”

“Tenacity” is key, said Calderwood, while Daniel Campos Pavoncelli, partner and producer at “My Brilliant Friend” outfit Indiana Productions, said that in a fickle market, producers need to identify the “one big selling point that will make a difference” — whether it’s an A-list star, a bankable director or an irresistible IP.

Still, some aspects of a historically chummy industry remain unchanged. “What we’re trying to do is leveraging relationships more than ever,” said Pavoncelli. “And that’s relationships with talent mostly, but also co-producers, buyers, broadcasters. Those relationships, which in our business are so important, then become vital.”

Italian production spend drops for first time since 2018

Investment in content production destined for Italy’s film, TV and streaming industries dropped 7.4% to €2 billion ($2.24 billion) in 2025, compared with the previous year, with the scripted sphere suffering most amid uncertainty over government support of the country’s tax credits and the ongoing transition in viewership from linear to streaming.

That was the main takeaway from a report issued by Italian TV producers’ association APA, which noted that this was the first decline in spend since 2018.

After reaping the rewards of a protracted growth spurt, Italian producers in 2025 faced a forced slowdown as the country’s right-wing government dithered with ongoing regulatory modifications to tax incentives for domestic film and TV production. The domestic tax credit modifications impasse did not impact Italy’s international production rebates, which remained firmly in place.

The report underlined that Italian scripted content continues to reach broad and demographically diverse audiences. In the linear broadcasting sphere, Lux Vide’s “Sandokan,” a modern take on the classic pirate tale adapted from Italian author Emilio Salgari’s iconic book series, and BiBiFilm’s “La Preside,” about a feisty female principal of a school in a crime-ridden Naples neighborhood, both drew a hefty average of over 4.6 million viewers per episode. In the streaming space, Picomedia’s Naples-set prison drama “The Sea Beyond” is still a big hit on state broadcaster RAI’s streaming and linear outlets, as is Aurora TV’s period drama “Il Paradiso delle Signore.”

The standout Italian original on Netflix is serial killer series “The Monster of Florence,” directed by genre specialist Stefano Sollima that launched from the 2025 Venice Film Festival and garnered 9.7 million global views in its first week in October 2025.

Finding the audiences — wherever they may be

Audiences are arguably consuming more content than ever before — just not in the ways that they used to, with YouTube, TikTok and other platforms competing for eyeballs alongside old-fashioned TV shows. So where does that leave drama producers? “Audiences are being really choosy about how they invest their time, and we need to up our game,” said “Black Mirror” and “Sharp Objects” executive producer Jessica Rhoades. “It is harder and harder to hit the bull’s eye,” agreed Anna Marsh, the CEO of Studiocanal and the deputy CEO and chief content officer for Canal+. When it comes to Gen Z audiences in particular, “there’s just no room for error.”

Gauging audience habits to thread that needle can be both art and science. Jamie Lynn, exec VP of co-production and distribution at Fremantle, expects to see more “razor-specific audience targeting” that will allow companies to develop projects for specific demos “at the right size and scale.” But producers and commissioners are bombarded with more viewing metrics than ever before; as Rhoades put it, “Listening to the audience too much is a fool’s errand.”

“We have a lot of data,” said Emanuele Marchesi, the director of Sky Studios Italia, the original programming and scripted television division of Sky Italia. “We have to find the courage to create new audiences.”

How to do that could just come down to good old-fashioned storytelling. “I like to think that we have the courage of our convictions,” said Andrew Plotkin, executive VP and head of drama development at Sony Pictures Television. “You never quite know how something’s going to be received, so all we can do is take something on that we feel passionate about. The audience is fickle. You never know what they’re going to connect with.”

This year saw the first edition of the MIA Market’s new European Investment Hub, which aims to help European industry professionals navigate the wide range of financial tools at their disposal and “foster direct contact between producers and representatives from these various entities who can provide guidance,” according to Tridente. Right on queue, Rome witnessed the launch this week of a €100 million ($112 million) fund — backed by Media Capital Technologies and Italy’s RP1 Holding — to finance audiovisual productions and film distribution in Italy and boost the country’s flagging indie sector.

From institutional investors and private-equity groups to brands and family offices, “there’s definitely more money in the marketplace than there ever has been in the 25 years I’ve been doing this,” said CAA’s Roeg Sutherland, who’s co-head of the agency’s media finance department and its international film group. For investors, the emergence of new formats and the booming creator economy offer inroads into the industry beyond the traditional realms of film and television. For producers, “I think we’re finding right now there are a range of international financing opportunities…[that] give you opportunities beyond the main U.S. and U.K. gatekeepers,” said Andrea Calderwood, of “Die My Love” producer Potboiler Productions.

Those opportunities can take myriad forms, from financing for an individual project or slate to an investment in a company that can catapult it to the next level. There’s no one-size-fits-all solution — either for the investors or their creative partners — and such arrangements, like any marriage, require give-and-take from both sides. Due diligence not only means having “your books ready” and being “realistic about your prospects” for a return on investment, according to Christopher Borde, managing director at the U.K.’s Media & Investment Advisors. It also means finding the right partner that’s aligned with your goals as a creative. “Know who you are and what you want to do,” said Celine Dornier, a content executive at Finland-U.K. based film investment fund IPR.VC.

It’s still early days for vertical content in much of the world, though a recent study projected that the format will generate $150 billion in revenue in global markets outside of China this year. In Europe, the interest — and investment — is rising, with German powerhouse Constantin Entertainment among the continent’s players entering the vertical market earlier this year. “Are we at an inflection point? I think the answer is yes, in terms of people’s cultural habits and why this might work now versus just 18 months ago,” said Andrew Plotkin, executive VP and head of drama development at Sony Pictures Television.

Digital platforms like YouTube and TikTok are beginning to invest in original vertical content, while legacy media companies are also leaning in, said former Netflix exec Kelly Luegenbiehl, founder of vertical video and microdrama outfit Shorties Studios. “Ultimately, what is their strategy going to be in this vertical space?” she asked, acknowledging that the burgeoning market is “definitely not for the risk-averse.” “It is definitely the Wild West. I think that there is no clear path for profitability — there’s no exact roadmap yet.”

It’s the prospect of getting in on the ground floor that makes vertical content so enticing, not only for investors but for creators. “Creativity is alive and well in the vertical space,” said Luegenbiehl, noting that without a playbook, her company has been “able to try things and take risks and move pretty quickly.” “In the vertical space, I like to say we’re in the business of yes,” she said, noting that the people driving the format’s growth are laying the groundwork for the successful industry to come. “If you build it, the audience will come.”

It’s been decades since the golden age of Dario Argento, Lucio Fulci and Mario Bava, but if there’s any doubt that Italian horror is enjoying a renaissance, look no further than Paolo Strippoli’s high-concept thriller “The Spiral,” which is repping Italy in the best international feature Oscar race. The talk during a lively MIA panel centered on some of the trends driving the current horror boom, from the rise of digital-native content creators to the eventizing of the theatrical experience and the “broadening beyond the elevated, arthouse horror that perhaps was only for a certain audience,” said Rachael Labes, manager of acquisitions and productions at horror streamer Shudder.

Savvy distributors are honing in on how to “create an aesthetic or a brand or a character that people want to seek out,” said Peter Kuplowsky, a producer and independent programmer for TIFF’s Midnight Madness strand. “You’re not just selling the one individual horror film. You’re selling the next film as well, and the idea that you want to create a brand around the filmmaker.”

Horror has always been a way to “discover new voices and [do] good business,” noted Andrea Romeo, founder and CEO of I Wonder, which released “Backrooms” and “The Substance” in Italy. So how to find the next “Backrooms”-style breakout? “TikTok’s definitely driving a lot of the conversation,” said Jonny Bunning, of “Faces of Death” and “It Ends” U.K. distributor Signature Entertainment. Kuplowsky said there’s a “gold rush” for YouTube and other online creators — “No one wants to get blamed that they missed something” — while Labes described “a frenzy toward finding the next Kane Parsons.” Still, “you can’t acquire a trend; you can only acquire a specific film or a specific director,” the Shudder exec noted. “Seeing the success and learning the lessons and investing in talent and letting a voice come through: That’s the lesson.”

Nick Vivarelli contributed reporting to this story.

#493. ‘Biermann’ Director Explains Why His Doc About a German Political Singer Is a Film for the Trump Era

Jens Meurer discusses his doc, screening at Austria's Viennale and showing Wolf Biermann narrating his life in various iterations of Germany, and how the outspoken artist inspired 'The Lives of Others.'

Biermann, the new documentary film from Jens Meurer (An Impossible Project, Public Enemy, Seaside Special), is a portrait of the outspoken political singer-songwriter and poet Wolf Biermann. Through the lens of his life, though, it also offers a cinematic reflection on the 20th-century history of Germany, Europe and the world. After all, Biermann has lived in five different versions of Germany.

Born in Hamburg in 1936, Biermann only met his father once – in prison before the Jewish communist was killed by the Nazis in Auschwitz. The doc shows how this experience gave Biermann his calling: to fight against injustice and for socialism. He moved to East Germany and made a name for himself as a critical and fearless voice in the GDR. To some, Biermann, who is still a close friend of Joan Baez’s, was like an East German Bob Dylan. The GDR regime banned him, forcing him to perform for 12 years in his East Berlin living room. When he played a concert in Cologne, West Germany, in 1976 in front of 7,500 people, the regime banned Biermann again – this time from re-entering East Germany. That saw the political artist live in exile in West Germany until he could visit the Eastern part of Germany again after reunification. Related Stories Business Nobody Knew This Game Existed, and Now It's a Hot 2027 Title TV 'MobLand' EP Teases What Season 3 Holds for Tom Hardy as 'Laird' Star Peter Sarsgaard Shares How He Feels About Playing a "Malevolent U.S. Billionaire"

Shot on 16mm film, Biermann follows the critical voice and father of 10 children as he narrates his David-versus-Goliath life, going through his everyday life, to performances and visiting to historic locations. It also features interviews with his contemporaries, including actor Armin Mueller-Stahl, who lauds his fire of rebellion but also calls him a “visible egomaniac,” and archive footage.

Biermann screens at the 64th edition of the Viennale, the Vienna film festival in Austria, which runs through Nov. 3, on Oct. 26 and Oct. 27, following its recent FilmFest Hamburg world premiere. Majestic Filmverleih will release the film in Germany, with Filmladen releasing it in Austria.

The Instant Film, Zeitsprung Pictures, Clouds Hill and zero fiction production was written by Dirk Kämper, Meurer and Biermann’s wife Pamela Biermann, who also appears in the film. Sebastian Ganschow and Bernd Fischer handled cinematography, with editing by Antje Lass, Zenon Kristen and Grete Jentzen.

Meurer talked to THR about how Biermann’s story relates to the Oscar-winning movie The Lives of Others, its timeliness in the age of Trump and why the songwriter’s messages are universal.

Wolf Biermann is well known in Germany, and his work is in German. But his story and work feel quite universal. What’s your take?

Yes, there is even an obvious Biermann pitch for an international audience, namely that the premise of The Lives of Others is based on his situation. It’s not his story, but Biermann’s apartment was the most observed apartment by the Stasi secret police in East Germany.

The original impetus for the film, to be honest, was to look at an incredible life story over a long German period. But as we got into the film, it became clearer and clearer that this is a film for today and about today. Biermann might turn 90 in two weeks, but he’s speaking to us very much also about the situation today.

I firmly believe this isn’t just a German story. At the very least, this is a European story, but it’s really a story for all of us in the world. It’s a story of somebody who stood up to power, who managed to speak his mind, express his opposition and speak for freedom, no matter what. And he did so not just in a brave manner, but also in a very humorous manner.

If I look at Trump, I think, “Where’s Charlie Chaplin!?” We should not be cowed. We should be making fun of these people, and that was Biermann’s biggest secret weapon – he attacked the dictatorship that he lived under with passion and humor. It’s an entertaining film – lots of laughter.

There is a scene in the film where Biermann goes back to East Germany after the fall of the wall and tells people that they didn’t speak out against the GDR regime enough, which underlines that what he tells us can be quite uncomfortable.

Yeah, he’s a real character. He gets a lot of resistance because he’s abrasive and doesn’t mince his words. He is – maybe that word is overused – authentic. It’s the kind of authenticity that we badly, badly need these days. And in that sense, he’s a secret weapon, and not just in Germany.

But what’s interesting is that he touches both people of his and my generation, but also young people who may not have heard his name before, but he speaks to them even more. I think there’s a thirst for that uprightness. His most famous song is called “Ermutigung,” or “Encouragement.” I think it’s what people are longing for and you get that with him, as you see in the film.

In the film, we see a woman mention that people have sometimes called Biermann the “Bob Dylan of Germany”…

The quote you’re referring to is really from the 1970s and from writer Barbara Honigmann, who said that for East Germans, he was their Bob Dylan. What she really means is that he was a figurehead; he was a leader in writing songs that spoke for people, that were original and that found words in a way that Bob Dylan did. They spoke to their generation; in Biermann’s case, the generation of opposition to this gray, boring and really terrible Stalinist dictatorship that they were living under.

Did you and Biermann know each other before you started work on the film? And how long did you film him?

No, it was a bit of a blind date. Somebody arranged for us to meet who thought there had been no documentary about him since 1982. There have been lots of TV interviews, but not a documentary. And somebody thought maybe these two would get along. We were introduced and hit it off very quickly. It was amazing to discover how much life there is in this 90-year-old.

We also hit it off because my approach is different. I shoot on film, and I do not do that for retro reasons or because it looks better or something like that. It’s the tool that I use to very respectfully, but veryrespectfully intrusively, get into people’s lives in a way so that we all enjoy the process. It’s very above board because you can’t hide a film camera, but it focuses everyone. That’s something that Biermann really appreciated. So, we filmed over the course of two years, and that led to a lot of time spent together, with and without camera. You have to choose your moments, working on film.

What was the most difficult thing about making Biermann?

The hardest part is that this is a 90-year-old German whose life [covers] a German century. He’s a Holocaust survivor who’s still a public and political force today. He’s currently on concert tour, filling large halls, for God’s sake! He’s somebody who’s had an incredible lifespan as a musician and as a poet. Biermann is actually Germany’s most published poet in the German language since World War II, and he’s still writing songs now.

He’s also on a concert tour, playing three-and-a-half-hour concerts this week. So, he’s still top fit. He is just a really great pianist, but he’s famous as a songwriter on the guitar.

For me, the film was also a discovery of his Jewish roots and of his communist roots all the way to the great role he played in changing German history with this expulsion from East Germany. He has lived in five Germanys. He grew up in Nazi Germany, lived in post-war occupied Germany, and then West Germany. He also moved to and lived in East Germany, and then [was sent back to West Germany] and now has been living in the reunited Germany. So one life, five Germanys.

There is no more German, European or world story in one person than his. If anyone thinks that this is just a German story, I think that’s a huge misunderstanding. This is such a larger-than-life, true-life story, and it’s such a universal message embodied in this extraordinary person.

Is there any particular inspiration that you feel Biermann and the man it is about can provide?

The man is 90, and he’s been through a lot, including having seen his father once in his life before he was murdered in Auschwitz. But he is still exuding a kind of optimism in spite of the shit show we are making our world into at the moment.

Something that I really want to capture in the documentaries I am making is this optimism. There’s plenty of room for films that tell the stories of all the challenges and woes that we are facing. Weirdly enough, it seems that there isn’t a big market for a film that also shows that maybe there is something positive in us, some agency. There’s definitely something in Biermann that also gives us cause for confidence that we are able to stand up, that each of us is able to do something. Biermann has a great line: Get fucking involved in your own life and in your own matters.

Just think of the David-versus-Goliath story of his life. He is a brilliant poet and songwriter but banned for 12 years. He couldn’t perform or be published in his own country for 12 years. So, he just recorded secretly, and his music was smuggled out into the West. So he was banned in East Germany but a best-selling musician in the West.

I think one great moment in the film is when he talks about his old apartment, and outside of it, there were all these trams, and they couldn’t edit them out of the recordings. So he just embraced them and said, “Those trams are my musicians.” And in West Germany, when people listened to these records, they said, “Oh man, that’s the great authentic sound of the East.”

I just started on a sequel of sorts to my film An Impossible Project. But this time around, it’s a “possible” project. It originates with the same [analogue enthusiast] character from Vienna, “Doc” [Florian Kaps], the guy who saved the last Polaroid factory in the world, against all odds.

He also got involved in saving vinyl, and he’s recently teamed up, after years and years of not really getting it right, to invent a new kind of vinyl recording machine. He teamed up with a totally fascinating Swedish company called Teenage Engineering. Together, they want to fight back and conquer America in a good way with a different kind of approach to what technology can be, namely that technology can also empower us as people, and not just enslave us.

#494. General Motors beats Wall Street's Q3 earnings expectations, narrows full-year guidance

DETROIT — General Motors narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-quarter expectations.

The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion after GM completed a $6 billion share repurchase program that was announced in January. GM did not disclose a specific time to complete the program.

Despite the positive news, GM stock fell nearly 7% during trading Tuesday as the company's outlook missed Wall Street's expectations.

Wall Street analysts were mixed before the report on whether GM would raise its guidance Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs. Analysts' expectations included a midpoint of $13.41 per share for the year compared with GM's new $13.25 per share midpoint, according to LSEG.

Several analysts in investor notes Tuesday said GM's third-quarter results were solid, but raised concerns about whether higher costs and pressures on vehicle pricing would limit earnings growth next year.

Here's how GM performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:

GM's new guidance includes adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, or $12.75 to $13.75 adjusted earnings per share, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of between $11.5 billion and $12.5 billion.

That compares with its raised guidance from July that included adjusted EBIT of between $14 billion and $16 billion, or $12 to $14 adjusted EPS, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion.

"I think the market's been pretty consistent from what we've said all year," GM CFO Paul Jacobson told CNBC's Phil LeBeau. "Our fourth quarter's going to be down sequentially. ... I think the fact that we're able to hold our guidance in the face of that late inflationary pressure in the year is another sign of the GM team executing really well."

GM on Tuesday said it expects commodity inflation costs to be around $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. That includes higher costs for logistics and dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, chips that are impacting multiple industries.

While the inflationary costs were at the automaker's high end of guidance, GM said its gross tariff costs are expected to be at the low end of its expected $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion range. Warranty costs are expected to be at high end between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, GM said.

Jacobson said vehicle pricing is relatively flat as inflationary costs continue to increase. He said the company would assess where consumers are in the coming year when deciding if it should pass costs along by raising prices more than normal.

"GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.

The automaker also said the costs of its pullback in all-electric vehicles announced last year were "substantially completed," saying it has recorded $11.2 billion in such charges since the second half of last year, including paying $4.6 billion of $7.4 billion in cash through the third quarter.

The company's net income attributed to stockholders was $3.3 billion during the third quarter, up roughly $2 billion from a year earlier.

GM's North American operations continued to lead the automaker's results, accounting for $3.6 billion of its $4.1 billion in adjusted EBIT results during the third quarter.

GM's 2025 third-quarter results included $48.59 billion in revenue, net income attributable to stockholders of $1.3 billion and earnings per share of $2.80 adjusted.

#495. Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain

Deep within the brainstem is a tiny group of nerve cells that plays an outsized role in how the brain functions. This region, called the locus coeruleus (LC), gets its name from the Latin words for "blue place." Although it contains only a small fraction of the brain's neurons, it produces norepinephrine (NE), a chemical messenger that helps regulate attention, learning, heart rate, and the body's reactions to stress and excitement.

Scientists have long assumed that the LC operates like a loudspeaker, sending essentially the same norepinephrine signal across the brain. However, a new study published in Nature challenges that understanding. Using brain imaging, recordings of neural activity, genetic techniques, and behavioral experiments in mice, researchers at the Allen Institute discovered that the LC communicates through several distinct pathways. Rather than broadcasting one general message, it delivers signals to specific destinations, with different groups of neurons responding to different experiences.

A Hidden Brain Network That Sends Precise Messages

By tracing the connections of LC neurons, researchers found that different groups of cells communicate with specific regions of the nervous system. These pathways determine where signals trigger the release of norepinephrine, creating a much more organized communication network than previously recognized.

Neurons in the upper (dorsal) portion of the LC primarily connect to the cerebral cortex and forebrain. Meanwhile, cells in the lower (ventral) portion send their signals mainly to the brainstem and spinal cord. This arrangement allows different parts of the LC to influence separate brain functions.

"The findings suggest the brain's norepinephrine system is far more like a targeted postal network than a foghorn," said Karel Svoboda, director of Neural Dynamics at the Allen Institute and study co-author.

Why the Discovery Could Matter for Brain Disorders

Understanding how this signaling network is organized could eventually change how certain neurological and mental health conditions are treated.

Norepinephrine plays a central role in regulating attention and mood, making it an important target for medications used to treat depression, anxiety, and ADHD. Neurons in the LC are also among the earliest brain cells to deteriorate in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the new findings could have implications for understanding and treating these conditions.

Current treatments that influence norepinephrine can affect multiple brain circuits at once, sometimes producing beneficial effects in one region while causing unwanted effects elsewhere. A clearer map of the LC's specialized pathways could help scientists develop therapies that act more selectively on the circuits involved in particular symptoms.

The research received support from the National Institutes of Health's Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies® Initiative, also known as The BRAIN Initiative®.

Scientists Identify Brain Cells Involved in Learning

The researchers also uncovered an important distinction between the functions of different LC neurons.

Cells in the dorsal LC that connect to the cortex were particularly active during learning. When mice performed decision-making tasks and adjusted their choices after an unfavorable result, these neurons increased their activity.

Neurons in the ventral LC behaved differently. Their activity rose shortly before mice ignored signals indicating that a reward might be available. This suggests that these cells help regulate whether animals respond to opportunities in their surroundings.

"What emerged was a clear map: neurons in the dorsal LC that send signals upward to the cortex are involved in learning, whereas neurons in the ventral region projecting downward to the brainstem and spinal cord govern whether animals engage with their environment at all," said Svoboda. "We also showed that these anatomical differences are mirrored by distinct gene expression patterns."

These findings indicate that the differences between the two groups extend beyond their locations and connections. They also have distinct patterns of gene activity that reflect their specialized roles.

Researchers Discover a Record-Breaking Neuron

The study involved an extensive examination of the mouse brain. Scientists used whole-brain imaging to study nearly 35,000 neurons, analyzed the genetic profiles of almost 400,000 cells, and reconstructed the complete structures of several exceptionally complex nerve cells.

During this work, they encountered another remarkable finding: LC neurons possess extraordinarily long axons. These projections carry signals from nerve cells to other cells, allowing information to travel across the nervous system.

The researchers found that LC axons measured approximately 35 centimeters long on average. One particularly extraordinary axon had a total reconstructed length of 70.32 centimeters, making it part of the longest single neuron ever measured in a mouse.

"This neuron, like many others that we studied, supplies NE to a very large volume of the cerebral cortex. For the brain, this is highly unusual. Most neurons are more specific in their targets," said Jeremiah Cohen, scientist at the Allen Institute and study co-author. "But this neuron doesn't release NE everywhere. It ignores the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord."

Despite its remarkable length and extensive reach, the neuron does not distribute norepinephrine throughout the entire brain. Instead, its connections remain selective, reinforcing the discovery that the LC operates through carefully organized signaling pathways.

A New Understanding of How the Brain Learns

The researchers also identified intriguing similarities between the norepinephrine system and the brain's dopamine signaling system.

Dopamine is another major chemical messenger that sends signals to the basal ganglia, a brain region involved in forming habits. Scientists suspect that dopamine and norepinephrine work together to support learning, potentially allowing the brain to acquire several complex and abstract concepts at the same time.

By revealing the intricate connections, specialized functions, and unusual physical structure of neurons in the locus coeruleus, the research provides a more detailed picture of how the animal brain communicates and learns.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice, they could eventually help scientists better understand human brain function and design treatments that target specific neural circuits rather than affecting entire signaling systems.

#497. China Renaissance suspends trading, delays results after founder's disappearance

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

#498. Avatar: Seven Havens finally shows us how Korra broke the world

Since Avatar Studios announced Avatar: Seven Havens, Avatar fans' biggest question has been, "How did Avatar Korra cause the apocalypse?"

In Seven Havens episode 7, we finally get closer to finding out.

The episode continues twin Avatars Pavi (voiced by Saheli Khan) and Nisha's (voiced by Aishu Devan) quest to find their parents. Their investigation brings them back to the mysterious glowing red anomaly that has plagued Ellora on and off throughout the season. It left behind a mass of crystals following its resurgence in the zombie-influenced "Night of the Afflicted," and when Pavi and Nisha tunnel beneath those crystals, they discover the ruins of what appears to be an old world factory. Based on the gear logo on the wall and an old mover showing Asami Sato cutting a ribbon outside the building, it's a Futures Industries factory.

Want more film and TV news and reviews delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable’s Top Stories newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

Deep in the bowels of the factory, Pavi finds a vast pit full of a strange liquid whose surface ripples with the glowing red design of the anomaly. As she makes contact with it, she's greeted with a memory of Republic City before the Cataclysm. The city has been completely rebuilt following the battle with Kuvira at the end of The Legend of Korra, in which Korra created a new spirit portal within the city's Spirit Wilds. Now, the yellow beam of that portal appears to emerge straight from a Future Industries tower, suggesting that the people of Republic City have built over or around the Spirit Wilds. That couldn't possibly have a negative impact on the physical world's relationship with the Spirit World, right?

In Pavi's anomaly vision, she also sees a concerned-looking Korra, one who's much older than when we last left her, flying from Air Temple Island to Republic City. When Nisha joins Pavi in the vision, the scene changes drastically. The twins find themselves in the city streets, surrounded by fires and explosions. As the smoke clears from a motorcycle crash, the twins see Korra again. This time, though, she's changed: She's in the Avatar State, and she sports a menacing smirk. That can only mean one thing. The twins are seeing the moment Korra somehow turned and broke the world.

As Pavi and Nisha look on, Korra reaches up to pipe-like structures running along Republic City's skyscrapers and tears them down. The breaking of the pipes unleashes massive bands of destructive purple energy beams, which look very similar to the spirit vine energy Kuvira harnessed in her campaign to conquer Republic City.

That's all we get of the Cataclysm, but there's already a lot to unpack here, from Republic City's new look to the purple energy beams. Most fascinating of all might be the pipe structures Korra is tearing down. Their design is not rigid and pipe-like, but instead resembles vines. In rebuilding Republic City, could its citizens have tried to harness spirit energy from the Spirit Wilds as an energy source? Did they build around the vines climbing up buildings, and if so, did that strategy backfire spectacularly, contributing to the Cataclysm? Based on Republic City's skyline and these mysterious pipes, it seems like the physical world's relationship with the Spirit World was already way out of whack by the time the Cataclysm happened. That's odd, given that much of Korra's time as the Avatar was focused on maintaining that balance. After all, she opened the spirit portals at the poles and in Republic City.

That brings us to Korra herself. Let's be totally real here. That smirking woman in the Avatar State might look like Korra and bend like Korra, but that frightening smile and the intent on destroying the world just doesn't feel like her. Obviously, a lot has changed since we last saw Korra on TV, but I refuse to believe she had an entire personality transplant!

Instead, this version of Korra in the Avatar State recalls a more sinister figure from Book 2 in The Legend of Korra. In the climax of that season, villain Unalaq merged with the darkness spirit Vaatu to create a dark Avatar whose eyes glowed red, contrasting with the white glow of the light spirit Raava, who lives within the Avatar. In the Seven Havens vision, Korra's eyes still glow white, yet her unsettling body language screams that the Avatar State has been corrupted in some way.

By the end of Season 2, Korra defeated Vaatu, but did not destroy him outright. Instead, his spirit is set to regrow within Raava over a period of 10,000 years, until the next Harmonic Convergence. That's a ways off within the Avatar timeline, but could the rapid acceleration of technology or Korra's proximity to the Spirit Wilds have accelerated that growth somewhat? Or alternatively, did some Future Industries technology create the anomaly and trigger some dark turn in Korra? I could very well be barking up the wrong spirit vine, but I have a feeling Book 2 of The Legend of Korra is about to become very, very important.

Clearly, we haven't gotten the full story yet, and Seven Havens is being very careful in how it doles out Korra's memories. In this episode alone, it leaves a gap between Korra's flight to Republic City and the Cataclysm. (Assuming the visions happen on the same night, that is, as Korra is wearing the exact same outfit in both.) That gap could be key to understanding Korra's motives in bringing on the Cataclysm, and hopefully in clearing her name somewhat in the timeline of Seven Havens.

#499. China's influence in the gaming industry is growing

Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."

Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.

#500. The Best Art TV Deals: Samsung Frame, Hisense Canvas, and More (2026)

We're big fans of art TVs here at WIRED. They're perfect for people who don't want a TV to be the constant center of attention in their living room. No art TV maker is better than the pioneer: Samsung. Specifically, Samsung's The Frame Pro series of TVs. The problem with The Frame Pro has always been the price. The smallest 55-inch model dropped to $1,098 during Prime Day earlier this month, and I've been happy to see that the price has stayed around. (In fact, earlier this week, it dropped by an additional $100 to its lowest price ever.) Seeing it discounted to under $1,000 was fantastic, but even at $1,098, it's a really solid deal. It was selling for $200 more in September and for the full retail price of $1,498 in August. Beyond the smallest 55-inch model, you also have size options for The Frame Pro of a 65-inch, 75-inch, or 85-inch TV.

Samsung also has an entry-level version of The Frame, which has an even deeper discount right now. It's just $898, which is $100 off its Prime Day price—the cheapest it's even been! It's actually the same price as the older 2025 model.

We haven't tested this model yet ourselves, but the main difference between The Frame and The Frame Pro is the brightness and image quality. They both use a matte finish, but The Frame Pro has nearly double the max brightness, while the standard Frame only goes up to around 650 nits. The Frame Pro also comes with a wireless connect box for a cleaner and simpler setup. It's definitely the one to get if you can swing the extra $200.

As we have documented, there's been an explosion of interest in art TVs in 2026, with competitors like Amazon, Hisense, and TCL joining the game. We've tested many of these new options—many of which try to undercut The Frame in price. The one on sale right now that I'd point to is the Hisense S7 CanvasTV (55S7SG). It's not even as bright as the standard Frame, but at $750 (for the 55-inch size), it's the cheapest art TV you can buy right now.

With Black Friday coming up next month, it's certainly possible that prices on these art TVs will drop even more. The 2025 Samsung Frame and Frame Pro both dropped to their lowest prices during Black Friday last year. It's a gamble—you could wait for Black Friday or get a sure thing right now.

#501. ‘Closure’ Director Michal Marczak Set for Narrative Feature Debut With ‘Perfection,’ About Hipster Millennials in Berlin (EXCLUSIVE)

The high-profile project is being unveiled on the sidelines of Rome's MIA market

Prominent Polish documentarist Michał Marczak – a Sundance Film Festival prizewinner with “All These Sleepless Nights” – is set to make his narrative feature debut with “Perfection,” a buzzy drama about hipster millennials in Berlin, based on Italian author Vincenzo Latronico’s eponymous novel that was shortlisted for the 2025 International Booker Prize.

German producer Roman Paul, of Razor Film (“Quo Vadis, Aida?”), Britain’s Andrea Calderwood, head of prominent London-based indie Potboiler Productions, and Italy’s Marta Donzelli, partner in Vivo Film (“The Last One for the Road”), have teamed up on the high-profile project. Donzelli was instrumental in winning the bidding war for the book’s rights that were negotiated with Claire Sabatié-Garat, who is Latronico’s literary agent. Popular on Variety Related Stories Emmys Move to Prime Video in Six-Year, Global Deal Worth Around $15 Million a Year

“Perfection” – which has been translated and sold in more than 40 countries – turns on a millennial expat couple named Anna and Tom who are living their dream during the 2010s in Berlin. “Their life as young digital creatives revolves around slow cooking, Danish furniture, sexual experimentation and the city’s 24-hour party scene – an ideal existence shared by an entire generation and tantalizingly lived out on social media,” says the synopsis of the book’s English-language edition.

“But beyond the images, dissatisfaction and ennui burgeon. Work becomes repetitive. Friends move back home, have children, grow up. Frustrated that their progressive politics amount to little more in practice than boycotting Uber, tipping in cash, or never eating tuna, Anna and Tom make a fruitless attempt at political activism,” it goes on to add. “Feeling increasingly trapped in their picture-perfect life, the couple takes ever more radical steps in the pursuit of an authenticity and a sense of purpose perennially beyond their grasp.”

“I’ve been living in Berlin since 1998 and with all the younger producers in my company – who are either expats or born there – we had long been looking for an original IP about what went on there in the 2010s when Berlin really meant something to the world,” Paul told Variety, speaking on the sidelines of the Rome MIA Market.

“In those early days of social media people were more idealistic about what it could achieve and how it allowed them to live the digital nomad life,” Calderwood said. “Because it is such a perfectly formed novel, we feel there is a way to make a perfectly formed film, which will have universal access and appeal,” she added.

Marczak, who won 2016 directing prize in the Sundance World Cinema – documentary category for “All These Sleepless Nights,” is known for his hybrid style that blurs the lines between documentary and fiction. His most recent work is multiple prize-winning “Closure,” about a teenager who disappears and his father’s relentless search for him, which also bowed at Sundance and will be released in U.S. theaters via 1-2 Special on Oct. 28.

Marczak’s films are “hybrid films, some of which focus on young people, for whom he has a very good eye and ear,” Paul noted, adding that “his sense of visuals is sublime.” He also pointed out that Marczak lived in Berlin and shot a film there, 2012 doc “Fuck for Forest” about a real-life Berlin-based non-governmental organization that raises money for environmental causes by producing and selling eco-pornography online.

Marczak and a still-to-be-determined screenwriter will write the English-language screenplay for “Perfection” that, unlike Latronico’s atmospheric novel, will include dialogues.

The producers are “in constant dialogue” with Latronico who “has been very supportive of our choice of director,” though the book’s author will not be directly involved in the screenplay, they said.

The “Perfection” project is in early development with Marczak attached as director, the next step being the writing of a treatment, followed by a screenplay.

“We are taking a step-by-step approach, building the development package before we take it to the market,” said Calderwood, who noted that “there is plenty of interest in the IP.”

Gosling and Shields were known for their spooky sound, with songs that centered on ghosts and monsters. #503. Best Buy launches new gaming hub ahead of 'Zelda' and 'Grand Theft Auto VI'

Best Buy is tapping further into a growing customer cohort: gamers.

Chief Revenue Officer Patrick McGinnis told CNBC exclusively that the electronics retailer is launching a new experience Tuesday for customers featuring gaming content, new technology and special offers, among other features. The online destination is called Best Buy Gamers and is launching in a beta version.

"Gamers are a customer that are really like no other in terms of their passion for not just the tech, the titles, but also how they want to work with each other as a community," McGinnis said. "So for us, being relevant for that customer wherever and whenever they want to interact with the thing that they love is really important."

Best Buy says millions of gamers shop at the retailer each year, including trying out games in the store and seeking advice from in-store experts. The new gaming experience, created in partnership with video game website IGN, will offer members gaming articles and reviews, live Best Buy event updates for launches and deals on new technology.

The announcement comes ahead of some of the biggest launches in gaming this year, including the Nov. 5 release of "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time," a remake from Nintendo, and the Nov. 19 launch of Take-Two Interactive's highly anticipated "Grand Theft Auto VI."

McGinnis said the timing of the rollout is "pretty perfect" given the slate of new video games over the next month, though Best Buy has been developing the new platform for over a year.

"We want to be relevant for our gaming customers, not just during the important, big tentpole periods of the calendar, like when we have these big gaming launches coming up, but really every day," he said. "We want to be there when they discover new titles and connect with the community, and not just when they're buying a big console or a new gaming title."

Best Buy has been leaning into gaming as it sees growing demand from its customers. For its fiscal first-quarter results reported in May, the company said gaming and computing was one of its biggest drivers of growth. On a call with analysts to discuss Best Buy's fiscal second quarter in August, incoming CEO Jason Bonfig said the company expects that demand for "Grand Theft Auto VI" will boost the gaming category.

Best Buy has been looking for growth drivers as the retailer tries to revitalize its business performance under Bonfig. The company has seen slumping sales and was hit by tariffs and lower consumer confidence, among other factors. Tapping into gaming could help revitalize the retailer.

McGinnis said the new gamer experience is an example of the company's strategic goals coming together.

"If you think about what those priorities are, the Gamers [beta] community is definitely a way that we're expanding and growing our reach, reaching that gaming customer," he said. "Providing a place for them to again pursue what they're most passionate about certainly is elevating our experience."

Best Buy is also leaning into in-store experiences around gaming, starting with a location in Torrance, California, next month, where Sony, Nintendo and Microsoft will come together to offer gaming experiences and activations for customers.

With the combination of physical retail and the online platform, McGinnis said, Best Buy hopes to sit at the intersection of technology, entertainment and culture within the gaming community. He said the company plans to tweak its new online experience based on feedback from its customers and continue innovating to meet its audience where it is, especially as the gaming segment continues to be one of the company's strongest performers.

"We recognize the gaming customer as incredibly passionate and wants to engage with what they love in a lot of different ways," he said. "There's observations of gaps that exist in the places and spaces where gamers are engaged, and we thought that we could build something that would really complement what they're engaging with today from a social platform perspective, not to replace those types of experiences in any way, shape or form."

The "eclipse of the century" will plunge some of ancient Egypt's most spectacular sites into darkness on Aug. 2, 2027. These temples, tombs and monuments are inside the path of totality.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027, has an ancient feel. It will certainly be a celestial event for the ages — at 6 minutes 23 seconds, it will feature the longest totality on land of the 21st century and the longest anywhere until 2114. However, its point of greatest eclipse occurs just a few miles from Thebes, the magnificent religious and political capital of ancient Egypt's Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom.

On the east bank of the mighty Nile is Luxor, the great city of the living, with its massive temple complexes of Karnak and Luxor. On its west bank is the city of the dead, which includes the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Hatshepsut. Modern Luxor, population 285,000, is set to become a focal point for eclipse chasers on Aug. 2, 2027, and will attract many thousands of international visitors. They'll come for the forecasted 0% chance of clouds and the era-defining duration of totality, but also to tour ancient Egypt's temples and monuments.

The chances of actually witnessing totality at any of the major temples are probably slim. Still, almost every eclipse chaser headed to Luxor will want to tour them before or after the eclipse. Visitors should be prepared for extreme August heat and check official opening and access arrangements before planning to watch the eclipse at any archaeological site. Certified eclipse glasses are essential during the partial phases; only during totality, when the sun is completely covered, is it safe to look without them.

Not all of ancient Egypt will experience totality. Egypt's top-ranking monument, the Pyramids at Giza, near Cairo, lies north of the path of totality and will get a 95% partial solar eclipse. Abu Simbel, on the shores of Lake Nasser south of Aswan, will also see a 92% partial solar eclipse. No matter, Luxor is home to some of the world's most impressive and well-preserved ancient monuments. Here are its temples, necropolises and palaces — and those nearby, also in the 160-mile (257-kilometer)-wide path of totality — that will have the moon's umbral shadow fall upon them on Aug. 2, 2027. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.

Start of totality and duration: 1:02 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

Dedicated to the god Amun-Ra — a fusion of the hidden god of the sun Amun and the ancient sun god Ra — this vast temple complex will be the hottest ticket in town for the eclipse. One of Egypt's most impressive and well-preserved ancient monuments, it's a place designed by ancient astronomers — the winter solstice sunrise still illuminates the innermost sanctuary. Access arrangements for eclipse day have yet to be confirmed, so keep an eye on official announcements before making plans to watch totality from the complex.

Start of totality and duration: 1:02 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

This is one of Egypt's best-preserved ancient temples and a must-see during the 2027 eclipse. It's on the banks of the Nile near the city center, so it's relatively easy to visit. Dedicated to the god Amun, it is known for its beautiful pillars and intricate carvings. A 75-foot (23 meters) tall obelisk on the east side of its entrance will point at the eclipsed sun almost directly overhead on Aug. 2, 2027. Its missing right-hand obelisk is in the Place de la Concorde, Paris.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

This incredible necropolis is home to the tombs of the pharaohs and is a testament to the advanced engineering and architectural skills of the ancient Egyptians. Of course, you don't want to be underground for totality, but some of the tombs are a must-see. Your tickets include entry to any three tombs of your choice from those open that day, with extra tickets available for the really impressive ones—the spectacular KV17 (Seti I), small but iconic KV62 (Tutankhamun), and KV9 (Ramesses V & VI). The latter's Corridor G has a ceiling decoration that may depict a deep partial solar eclipse from 1143 BC.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

If one temple is best suited to crowds for an eclipse, it's this vast, open-air gem dedicated to the legendary queen who became pharaoh. However, with almost no shade, it could be the least practical option. Three huge terraces rise above the desert floor and into the cliffs of Deir el-Bahari to the west. It's an absolute masterpiece.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

This is where we get to temples that are fairly well known, but likely won't have as much pressure on them from eclipse chasers as the big three — Karnak, Luxor and Hatshepsut. However, anyone looking for ways to get temple architecture into images of an eclipse at zenith should look no further than these two large stone statues of Pharaoh Amenhotep III. Behind them are the ruins of the largest temple in the Theban Necropolis.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

Getting off the beaten track in August 2027 will be near-impossible, but here's an option — the Mortuary Temple of Ramesses III. Featuring towering stone columns, colorful reliefs (despite being 3,200 years old) and famous carvings, it's bypassed by tour buses heading straight for Hatshepsut.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 19 seconds

Another temple that, without Karnak and Luxor nearby, would be rammed with visitors, is the Ramesseum — the mortuary temple of Ramesses II. Featuring the remains of a huge fallen statue that inspired Shelley's poem Ozymandias, it's in an area once used by the artisans who built the royal tombs, and slightly off the tourist route.

Start of totality and duration: 1:02 p.m. EEST; 5 minutes, 47 seconds

If you want to avoid the scrum of eclipse chasers in Luxor on and around Aug. 2, the Temple of Khnum could be an option. Located in Esna, about 34 miles (55 kilometers) south of Luxor, the so-called 'Rainbow Temple' (for its colorful ceilings) is dedicated to the ram-headed creator god Khnum. Dating from the Greco-Roman era, there's a vast Hypostyle Hall that sits below modern street level, which could be good for some shade.

Start of totality and duration: 1:01 p.m. EEST; 6 minutes, 15 seconds

If you want to escape Luxor but (almost) keep its long totality, head to Qena, 40 miles (65 km) north, where one of Egypt's best-preserved and most beautiful temples stands. Dendera was the cult center for Hathor, one of the most important and popular deities in ancient Egypt and known as the 'lady of the sky.' The temple's entrance has six massive columns, each decorated with Hathor's head, and its ceiling features astronomical engravings.

Start of totality and duration: 1:04 p.m. EEST; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Another great option for those who prioritize ancient Egyptian surroundings over the longest possible totality is the Temple of Horus, one of the most striking and best-preserved temples in ancient Egypt. About 68 miles (110 km) south of Luxor, it's dedicated to the sun and sky god Horus, one of the main gods in ancient Egypt, whose right eye represents the sun and left eye the moon. The temple's stone roofs are intact, so its Hypostyle Halls, inner chambers and central sanctuary provide some shade.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#505. Yaga isnt the show Hudson Williams fans want it to be

There's so much to want to love in Canadian series Yaga, from its small-town mystery to its hints of folklore and witchcraft. But the biggest draw of all is undoubtedly its cast, which includes Carrie-Anne Moss, Noah Reid, Clark Backo, and Heated Rivalry breakout Hudson Williams.

Yaga is Williams' first major project to come out since the runaway success of Heated Rivalry catapulted him and co-star Connor Storrie to stardom. With that comes an opportunity for Williams to further showcase his range beyond his Canadian Screen Award-winning work as Shane Hollander. It's a shame, then, that Yaga gives Williams and his co-stars so little to latch onto, in a dark feminist fable that feels more hollow than revelatory.

Want more film and TV news and reviews delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable’s Top Stories newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

Based on the play by Kat Sandler, who also serves as showrunner, Yaga invites us to the small town of Whittock, where Henry Park (Williams), heir to a powerful fishery owner, has gone missing. Enter private investigator Rapp (Reid) and local police detective Carson (Backo), who are paired — reluctantly, on Carson's end — to get to the bottom of this mystery.

What begins as a standard missing persons investigation soon becomes something darker and stranger. Chicken carcasses hang menacingly on doors. Bloody symbols mar crime scenes. Through it all, Rapp hears whispers of Baba Yaga, a legendary witch from Slavic folklore known for living in a house on chicken legs and flying around in a mortar and pestle. Could Henry's disappearance be tied to the occult? Given that the whole series opens with images of an unknown figure being burned at the stake, and that each episode opens and closes with a voiceover monologue from a wizened witchy figure, the answer appears to be an unequivocal "yes."

So the stage is set for a strange, folkloric mystery. Yet Yaga's witchiness never truly sings. Too often, the show resorts to the same style of surreal fakeout dream sequences, where a stream of bloody feathers and foreboding masks blends into a shorthand for horror without truly scaring. The voiceovers, presented as coming from Baba Yaga herself, offer up platitudes about women who have been othered as witches, but they feel familiar to anyone who's ever read a "we are the granddaughters of the witches you couldn't burn" bumper sticker.

At the center of this witchy vortex is Williams' Henry, who mostly haunts Rapp and Carson's investigation in flashbacks, including a steamy podcast recording with him and intriguing professor Katherine (Moss), an expert in all things bone. Henry's not alone: Williams also plays Logan, Henry's roommate, podcasting partner, and doppelganger. (Yaga sticks Williams in a prosthetic nose and fake acne for the Logan role, and the result is a jarring trip to the uncanny valley.)

A dual role should be rich territory for any actor to mine, yet neither Henry nor Logan get enough screen time for Williams' double turn to truly sink in. Henry is primarily a confident, if sleazy, charmer, while Logan is mostly presented as an awkward, almost wooden foil to that charm. Logan was not a character in the original stage play, and it shows in his thinness here.

Yaga introduces a fascinating thread about Logan perhaps wanting to be (or maybe be with) Henry, but it rarely pulls it beyond the occasional unsettling sex scene. While onscreen intimacy can often be a great showcase of character dynamics, here, these scenes are often over too fast or accompanied by a voiceover that explains said dynamics without letting the actual performances breathe.

As Yaga unfurls, Henry and Logan become much more sinister figures. While the thought of Williams taking a villainous turn is an exciting one, his Henry and Logan don't make particularly compelling villains because we know so little of them. Yaga's leads don't tend to fare much better. Moss is slippery fun as Katherine, but too often she remains on the margins. Backo and Reid's buddy cop dynamic is punchy, yet often dragged down by Rapp's incessant flirting. That most of the women in Whittock practically throw themselves at him is one of Yaga's most infuriating features. As it happens again and again and again, these women's advances bypass sexual empowerment and move straight into bewilderment.

Yaga gestures out to interesting concepts, but ultimately, it never dives deep enough. As an examination of witchcraft as a conduit for female rage, it's not angry enough. As an erotic thriller, it's not titillating enough. As a mystery, its twists and turns are intriguing, but never quite captivating. The ingredients for success are there, but they never quite come together to cast the right spell.
